<!-- https://docustay.app -->
# The e-signature API you own. One flat price for every user.

Open source and self-hostable. Pro is $35 a month for your whole team: no per-seat fees, unlimited people and documents. Signers can pay while they sign, straight into your own Stripe account, and Pro adds no fee.

Send from your code, get documents signed on any device, and keep a sealed PDF with a certificate of completion. Self-host it under the AGPL-3.0 or use the hosted service.

- [Try the demo](/demo) (no sign-up; nothing is ever sent)
- [Read the docs](/docs)

## Integrate this afternoon

Make a test key, post a template and one signer, and listen for one webhook. A key that starts dsk_test_ only does practice runs.

```
curl -X POST "$DOCUSTAY_URL/api/v1/documents/send" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DOCUSTAY_API_KEY" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: $(uuidgen)" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"templateId":"$DOCUSTAY_TEMPLATE_ID","parties":[{"seat":"signer_1","name":"Rosa Alvarez","email":"rosa@example.com"}]}'
```

## Why developers choose Docustay

- **You can read it.** The server, the app and the signing page are open source under the AGPL-3.0.
- **You can run it.** Three commands start your own copy; your documents stay on your server.
- **Safe to build against.** A test key emails only you, stamps pages TEST and never counts toward a limit.
- **Written down, not promised.** One OpenAPI 3.1 file; the reference and the clients are generated from it.
- **Made for agents.** An MCP server and a Claude plugin; a draft-only key can prepare documents but cannot send them.
- **AI that stays in its lane.** Scribe drafts and checks; a person approves every send.
- **Money inside signing.** The signer can pay as part of signing, into your own Stripe account.
- **Proof you can check without us.** Every signed PDF carries a certificate of completion with a hash; the verify page needs no account.
- **Pay for what you use.** Free is 15 documents a month; Pay as you go is $5 per team member; Pro is $35 for the whole workspace.

## More

- [Developers](/developers)
- [How it works](/features/how-it-works)
- [Templates](/free-templates)
- [Pricing](/pricing)
- [Self-host](/self-host)
- [Trust](/trust)

Docustay is not for protected health information yet.

# Every step, from a file to a sealed copy.

All the e-signature features, from creating a document to a sealed copy: send it, get it signed on any device, get paid and keep proof. All of it works in the app and from your code.

## Five steps, one flow.

1. **Create**: Template, PDF or words
2. **Send**: Who signs, in what order
3. **Sign**: Any device, no account
4. **Get paid**: Inside the signature
5. **Prove**: Sealed PDF + certificate

## One page for each thing Docustay does.

Send and sign, get paid and use AI, and make it yours. Open any of them for the details, the limits and the questions people ask.

**How it works.** The whole flow, from creating a document to the sealed copy.

**Signing.** What the signer sees: any device, no account, drawn or typed.

**Templates and sending.** Text tags, field detection, the library and sending to a list.

**Proof and verify.** A certificate with every signed copy, and a verify page that needs no account.

**Payments.** The signer pays as part of signing, into your own Stripe account.

**Scribe.** Describe a document in plain words and review what Scribe builds.

**AI agents.** Let an assistant draft. A person approves the send.

**Your brand.** Your logo and your colours on the signing page.

**Embedded signing.** Show the signer inside your own product.

**Team and roles.** Owner, Admin and Member, and what each costs.

**Test mode.** A full sandbox where nothing reaches a real inbox.

## You do not need to write code.

**Pick or upload.** Start from a template or upload a PDF and drop the fields on it.

**Say who signs.** Add names and emails, choose the order and press send. People sign on any phone with no account.

**Keep the proof.** Everyone gets the sealed copy and its certificate, and you can check any copy later.

## Free, Pay as you go and Pro.

| What you get | Free | Pay as you go | Pro |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Documents a month | 15 | 15 free, then $0.50 each | Unlimited |
| AI drafts a month | 10 | 10 free, then $0.30 each | 100, then $0.30 each |
| Team members who can send | One, the owner | $5 per team member a month | Everyone, at no extra charge |
| Signers | 15 different signers a month | Unlimited, free | Unlimited, free |
| New templates a month | 5 | 25 | Unlimited |
| API, webhooks and test mode | Included | Included | Included |
| Reminders and send to a list | Included | Included | Included |
| Your own plays and playbooks | No | No | Yes |
| Fee on payments taken while signing | 2% | 2% | 0% |

## Pick the feature that matches your day.

If you send a few documents a week, start with How it works and Templates: pick a template, add the people and press send. Everything works from the app, and the demo lets you try it with no sign-up.

If you are building signing into a product, start with Test mode and Embedded signing, then read the developer pages. A test key lets you build the whole flow before a real person gets an email.

If you want an assistant to do the typing, start with Scribe and Agent-ready. They draft, and a person approves every send.

## What is behind the features.

Every figure on this page is checked against the code on the date shown on the About page.

- **64** API operations: One OpenAPI 3.1 file.
- **39** MCP tools: For an assistant that drafts.
- **12** API scopes: A key can be given only what it needs.
- **600** Requests a minute: The same limit on every plan.

## A document's life, as your code hears it.

- Sent: documents.document.sent
- Opened: documents.document.opened
- Signed: documents.document.signed
- Executed: documents.document.executed

## Three ways teams use it.

**A signing step in your product.** Your server asks for a session, your page shows the signer, and your code hears the completed event. The signer never leaves your site.

**Paperwork without a developer.** A property manager picks the lease addendum, adds the tenant, sends it and keeps the sealed copy. No code, no account for the tenant.

**An assistant that drafts.** An agent prepares the document from a template and a person reads it and presses send.

## The documentation behind each feature.

Every page above has a matching guide for the people who build with it.

- [Quickstart](/docs/quickstart): A test key, a send and a webhook in about ten minutes.
- [Templates and text tags](/docs/templates-and-text-tags): Write fields into a file and they place themselves.
- [Payments in the API](/docs/search-and-payments): List payments and refund with a reason.
- [Embedding](/docs/embedding): The elements, the allow list and the events.
- [MCP and the Claude plugin](/docs/mcp-and-skills): Connect an assistant and set a draft-only key.
- [Test mode](/docs/test-mode): Keys, watermarks and the listen command.

## Questions

**Do the features work from the API as well?**

Yes. Everything in the app has an API call, and the same events reach your webhooks.

**Is there a free plan?**

Yes. Free covers real work: 15 documents a month, with test mode, the API and webhooks.

**Can I try it without an account?**

Yes. The demo gives you a real workspace for 24 hours with no sign-up, and nothing in it is ever emailed.

**Do I need to write code to use any of this?**

No. Every feature on this page works in the app, and the demo lets you click through it with no sign-up. The API, SDKs and command line are there for the day you want to put signing inside your own product.

**What does it cost?**

Free is 15 documents a month with test mode, the API and webhooks. Pro is one flat price for the whole workspace, and the page for pricing has the full table.

<!-- https://docustay.app/features/how-it-works -->
# From a file to a sealed copy.

See how e-signatures work, step by step: create a document, send it, get it signed on any device, get paid and keep proof anyone can check. Every step works in the app and from your code.

## Five stages, one flow.

1. **Create**: Template, PDF or words
2. **Send**: Order and reminders
3. **Sign**: Any phone
4. **Get paid**: Inside signing
5. **Prove**: Sealed + certificate

## Start from a template, a PDF or a sentence.

Pick one of 54 templates, upload a PDF and let Find fields place the boxes, or tell Scribe what you need. Then drag each field to where it belongs and give it to a signer.

**Find fields.** Docustay reads a PDF and proposes the signature, date and text boxes. You move or remove any of them.

**Fields.** Signature, initials, date, text, checkbox, dropdown, picture and payment, each given to one signer.

## Say who signs, and in what order.

Add each person by name and email. Send to one person, to a line of people one after another, or to everyone at once. The next person is told only when it is their turn.

**Order.** One at a time or all together, and you can change it before you send.

**Reminders.** Reminders go out until the document is signed, and you set when it expires.

**Send to a list.** Upload a spreadsheet and send one document to each row. Free sends up to 15 at a time.

**Your name.** The email comes from Docustay with your name and your reply-to address.

## Sign on any phone, with no account.

The signer opens the link, reads, fills in what is theirs and signs with a finger or a mouse. It works on any phone or computer.

**No account.** Nothing to install and nothing to sign up for.

**Decline.** A person can decline and say why, and you are told at once.

**Embedded.** Show the same page inside your own product.

## The signer pays as part of signing.

Add a payment field and the signer pays on the same page, straight into your own Stripe account. Docustay checks the amount and never holds the money. The fee is 2% on Free and Pay as you go and 0% on Pro, on top of Stripe's.

**Amount.** One amount you set, paid in full while signing. A deposit is just a smaller amount.

**Fee.** Docustay's fee is 2% on Free and Pay as you go and 0% on Pro.

## Keep a sealed copy that anyone can check.

When everyone has signed, Docustay seals the PDF and adds a certificate of completion: who signed, when, from where, and a hash of the file. Anyone can check a copy with no account.

**Sealed.** The whole file is sealed, so a later change shows.

**Record.** Every action has its time, and the audit trail stays with the document.

**Verify.** Drop a copy on the verify page and get an answer.

## The same flow in two commands.

Send a test document and listen for what happens to it. A test key emails only you and stamps the document TEST.

```
npx docustay login
npx docustay send --test $DOCUSTAY_TEMPLATE_ID --party signer_1="Rosa Alvarez <rosa@example.com>"
```

## Reminders until it is done.

- Day 0: Sent
- Day 3: Reminder
- Day 7: Reminder
- Day 14: Signed, reminders stop

## Email that comes from you.

Documents and emails carry your logo and colour, and every email goes out under your name with your reply-to address. For one document, change the subject and the message on the Details step.

- Your sender name and reply-to address on every email.
- A send-me-a-test button before anything goes out.

## More than signers.

**Signers and approvers.** A signer fills in fields and signs. An approver says yes before the next person is asked, so a manager can clear an offer letter first.

**Viewers and copy-only.** A viewer can read the document, and a copy-only person gets the finished copy without signing.

**An assistant for someone else.** A person can fill in fields on behalf of a signer, such as a receptionist helping at a counter, and the record says so.

## Every stage leaves a record.

| Stage | Who acts | What is kept | What your code hears |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Create | You, or Scribe for you | The document, its fields and who each belongs to | documents.document.created |
| Send | You | Who was sent what, in which order, and when | documents.document.sent |
| Open | The signer | The time, the address and the browser | documents.document.opened |
| Sign | Each signer | The wording they agreed to and a hash of each signature | documents.document.signed |
| Seal | Docustay | The sealed PDF and the certificate of completion | documents.document.executed |
| Stop | You or the signer | Who declined, voided or let it expire, and why | documents.document.declined |

## Eight events cover the whole life of a document.

- Created: documents.document.created
- Sent: documents.document.sent
- Opened: documents.document.opened
- Signed: documents.document.signed
- Executed: documents.document.executed
- Declined: documents.document.declined

## The same flow, wherever you start.

**In the app.** Pick a template, add the people and press send. Everything on this page is a screen you can click through in the demo.

**From your API.** Each stage is one call, and every call can be tried with a test key that emails only you.

**Through an assistant.** An agent can prepare the document and a person approves the send.

## Your documents, your record.

Every signed document is stored with its audit trail, and everyone who signed was emailed a copy. You can download the sealed PDF again from the document page or with one API call.

On the hosted service the files are encrypted at rest. If you run Docustay on your own server, the files stay on that server and nothing is sent to us.

## Questions

**Does the signer need an account?**

No. They open the link and sign.

**Can I do this without writing code?**

Yes. Everything on this page works in the app, and the demo lets you try it with no sign-up.

**Who can see the signed copy?**

Everyone who signed is emailed a copy, and you keep it with its audit trail in your workspace.

**Can I stop a document after it is sent?**

Yes. You can void it, and anyone who was asked to sign is told it was cancelled. A document can also expire on the date you set, and the sender is told when it lapses unsigned.

**Can signers decline?**

Yes. A person can decline and say why, and you are told at once. The decline is part of the record.

- [Proof and verify](/features/proof)

<!-- https://docustay.app/features/scribe -->
# Describe it. Scribe builds it.

Scribe is the AI document builder in Docustay. Tell it what you need. It asks a few clickable questions, writes the document, places every field and sets the payment terms. It drafts. A person sends.

## AI that drafts, never sends.

**A person approves.** Nothing leaves the workspace until you read the draft and press send.

**The same through MCP.** An assistant on the MCP server can prepare documents but cannot send one. A draft-only key makes that a rule, not a promise.

**Checked first.** Scribe reads a document for missing fields, a signer with no email and terms that contradict each other, and tells you what it found.

## It uses what you already have.

**Your templates.** Scribe looks in the template library first, asks that template's own questions and says which one it used.

**Your PDFs.** Upload a PDF and Scribe reads it, finds where the fields belong and proposes them for you to move or remove.

**Your Plays.** A Play is a reusable instruction for one kind of document, and a Playbook is a set of them. Your own are on Pro.

## Say what you are collecting. Code places the field.

When Stripe is connected, Scribe's wizard asks for the amount, the currency, who pays and what it is for. The AI drafts the document around those values. Code checks them, writes the payment terms from your own values and places the one payment field.

- The AI never sets an amount. If it writes a payment field of its own, that field is thrown away.
- You review the draft before anything is sent.
- Stripe must be connected first. Payments are powered by Stripe.

## From your words to a finished document.

1. **You describe**: In plain words
2. **Scribe asks**: Clickable questions
3. **Scribe builds**: Text + fields
4. **You review**: Nothing sent yet
5. **Send**: When you approve

## What Scribe does for you.

**Asks.** A few questions with two to four options each, so you click instead of typing.

**Writes.** A full document in plain words, in sections you can edit.

**Places fields.** Signature, date and every other field, each given to the right person.

**Sets payment terms.** Amounts and dates, once your Stripe account is connected.

## Start from a template.

Scribe looks in the template library first, asks the template's own questions and says which template it used. Built-in Plays are free; your own Plays and Playbooks are on Pro.

- Pick a built-in template and answer its questions.
- Write your own Plays, and call the library from your code with the API.

## What a draft costs.

- **Free**: 10 AI drafts a month
- **Pay as you go**: 10 drafts a month, then $0.30 each
- **Pro**: 100 drafts a month, then $0.30 each
- **Lifetime**: 50 drafts a month, then $0.30 each

- **Price first**: The price of a draft is shown before you use it
- **Never charged**: A failed or empty draft is never charged
- **Review**: You approve every document before it is sent
- **Nothing alone**: Scribe never sends by itself

## Describe it. Review it. Send it.

**You say what you need.** Describe the document in plain words. Scribe asks a few clickable questions.

**It places every field.** Signature, date and every other field, each given to the right person.

**You approve, then it sends.** Payment terms are set once your Stripe account is connected. Nothing is sent until you approve.

## You decide. Scribe does the typing.

| Step | You | Scribe |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Say what you need | In plain words | Asks a few clickable questions |
| Write the document | Edit any section | Writes it in sections you can change |
| Place the fields | Move or change any of them | Gives each person their signature, date and other fields |
| Send it | Approve it | Never sends by itself |

Scribe is a drafting aid. It is not legal advice, and you review every document before anything is sent.

## What Scribe asks before it writes a word.

| Question | How you answer |
| --- | --- |
| What is this for, in plain words? | Free text. |
| Who are the parties, and who signs? | Free text. |
| Who signs first? | No order, or one after another in the order listed. |
| What does each side provide? | Free text. |
| Money terms and dates | Free text. Amounts and dates come from you only; anything left out becomes a blank someone fills in. |
| Which state or country's law applies? | Free text. Left blank, it becomes a blank to fill in. |
| What does the signer fill in? | Free text. |
| How long do they have, and when to remind? | Free text. |

Then the questions for the kind of document: an NDA, a lease addendum, a photo release, a services agreement, a contractor agreement, a consent or waiver form, an offer letter or a deposit agreement.

## What Scribe never does.

- **Send, pay, sign**: Scribe never sends a document, never pays and never signs. Over MCP, nothing is emailed until send_draft is called again with confirm set to true.
- **Changes are proposals**: An edit request returns proposed changes (replace_text, insert_block, replace_block or remove_block) for a person to accept. It never returns an edited document.
- **Money is yours**: The amount of a payment comes only from the person. Plain code, not the model, checks every amount it proposes against yours and places one payment field for the payer.
- **Progress**: A draft job moves from queued to writing, checking and ready, or failed. It can be cancelled, and a job whose worker died is put back and finished by itself.
- **Off by default**: An owner switches AI drafting on for the workspace, and can set a second reader for each draft, require the sender to read it before sending, add house rules and cap drafts a day and a month.

## Ask for a draft and poll for the result.

A draft is a suggestion for a person to read: nothing is saved or sent.

```
curl -X POST https://docustay.app/api/v1/documents/ai/draft \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DOCUSTAY_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "prompt": "A one-page services agreement with a client signature", "mode": "template" }'
```

## Pick a writer, see the price.

**Three writers.** Plain-language writer (short sentences, no jargon), Careful contract drafter (precise terms, defined words, every risk named) and Quick forms (short forms and notices, fast).

**Drafts.** Free includes 10 AI drafts a month and Pro includes 100. Past that a draft is $0.30 on a paid plan, shown before you use it.

**Ten currencies for payments.** The wizard offers usd, eur, gbp, cad, aud, nzd, chf, sek, nok and dkk. A document with a payment can only be sent when Stripe is connected.

## Keep going with the next piece.

- [Templates](/free-templates): Scribe finds the right built-in template and reads its guidance.
- [Payments](/features/payments): Payment terms are set once Stripe is connected.
- [Developers: agents](/developers/agents): The MCP server and the connector.

## Questions

**Is Scribe legal advice?**

No. It writes a starting point and flags only small things that matter. You review every document before it goes out.

**Can I change what it writes?**

Yes. Review it, edit the text or any field, then send.

**Does Scribe send anything by itself?**

No. Nothing is sent until you approve it.

**What is a draft?**

One request that makes a document from your words or a file. Free includes 10 a month and Pro includes 100. Past the allowance a draft is $0.30 on a paid plan, and a failed or empty draft is never charged.

<!-- https://docustay.app/features/proof -->
# Proof anyone can check.

The certificate of completion on the last page of every signed PDF lists who signed and when. The whole file is sealed, so a later change shows, and anyone can verify a copy with no account.

## Four things travel with the file.

**The seal.** A digital seal over the whole PDF, so any later change shows.

**The fingerprint.** A SHA-256 hash of the document, printed on the certificate.

**The record.** Each action with its time, address and browser, kept with the document.

**The signers.** Each person's name, email and role, and the wording they agreed to.

## Five layers, one sealed file.

The page, the fields, the signatures, the seal and the certificate are one PDF. Change any layer and the seal no longer matches.


## Every step, with its time. Every signature, with its hash.

- Sent: 09:14
- Opened: 09:17
- Signed: 09:20 · hash c093
- Sealed: 09:58 · hash 9f2c

## What the certificate shows, and how to check it.

- **Who**: Each person's name, email and role
- **When**: The time of each action, local and UTC
- **From**: The address and browser of each action
- **Agreed**: The exact wording they agreed to
- **Fingerprint**: A hash of the document, so a change shows

- **Drop**: A signed PDF onto the verify page
- **Check**: The seal is valid and the file is unchanged
- **Read**: Who signed, and when
- **Private**: The check runs in your browser; the file is not uploaded

## Change one letter and the chain breaks.

In the signature record, each hash covers its own text and the hash before it. Edit any record below and watch every later record stop matching.


## What a Docustay signature is, and what it is not.

- **Kind**: A simple electronic signature with a strong record and a digital seal
- **Record**: Intent, consent, who, when, from where, and the file's hash
- **Seal**: A digital signature over the whole file, with a trusted timestamp when the time service answers

- **Qualified**: Not a qualified electronic signature
- **Identity**: No identity documents or knowledge checks
- **Advice**: No legal advice and no promise about any outcome

## The last page tells the whole story.

It lists who signed, when, and a hash of the file, on the PDF itself. It does not need Docustay to be read.

**Who and when.** Each person's name and the time of each signature.

**The fingerprint.** A hash of the document, so a later change shows.

## Every step is a row you can export.

Sent, opened, signed, sealed: each is written down with its time, and the whole log downloads as a CSV.

**Same names.** The events are the ones webhooks send, so your system and the record agree.

## You do not have to take our word for it.

Drop a signed PDF on the verify page. It checks the seal in your browser, with no account, and says whether the file is intact, whether it carries a trusted timestamp, and what its fingerprint is. Who signed and when is on the certificate page inside the file.

The seal is a digital signature over the whole file. If anyone changes the file afterwards, it no longer matches.

## Three checks, and what they do not prove.

The verify page re-reads the signature inside the PDF. A forger who only copies the right digest into a fake signature fails the second check.

- **1 · The digest**: The digest the signer signed must equal the digest of the file's signed byte ranges.
- **2 · The signature value**: The signature over the signed attributes must verify with the public key of the certificate inside the file.
- **3 · The end of the file**: The last signed range must reach the end of the file, or what follows is only Docustay's own validation material. A page appended after sealing fails.
- **Whose seal**: The verifier reports the certificate that sealed the file and says known when its fingerprint is on Docustay's published list, unknown otherwise.
- **What it does not say**: The seal is a self-signed certificate. A pass means this exact signature was made by that key over this exact file. It does not mean an outside authority vouches for who signed.

## What the certificate can show, and what you can leave off.

| Part | What is printed | Owner setting |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timeline | Each step in time order: sent, opened, reminded, agreed to sign, signed, completed. | On or off |
| Network address | The address each signer opened and signed from. | On or off |
| Device and browser | The device each signer used. | On or off |
| Document fingerprints | A hash of the original file. | On or off |
| Consent record | That each person agreed to sign electronically: the version, time, address and device. | On or off |
| Closing statement | A sentence at the bottom saying the document was sealed with a digital signature when the last party signed. | Editable, up to 600 characters |

Also on it when they apply: the reason a person gave, who a seat was passed on from, what each signer paid with Stripe's reference, and a signature ID. The certificate is the last pages of the PDF, or a second sealed PDF if you switch that setting.

## Evidence you can hand to someone else.

**The evidence package.** Once a document is executed, a team member can download one zip: original.pdf, signed.pdf, audit-log.csv, evidence.json and a README. evidence.json lists every signature with its hashes and every file with its SHA-256.

**A signature ID.** The first 12 characters of a signature record's own hash, in three groups of four, printed beside the signature when the owner turns it on. Anyone can recompute it from the record.

**How long it is kept.** Signed documents stay in your workspace, and you can download the sealed copy and its audit log at any time.

## Download the sealed copy from your own code.

```
curl https://docustay.app/api/v1/documents/$DOCUSTAY_DOCUMENT_ID/signed.pdf \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DOCUSTAY_API_KEY" -o signed.pdf
```

## On your own server, the seal is yours.

A self-hosted install makes a signing certificate for itself at first run. Set your own to use one from a trusted authority, and point it at a timestamp authority so finished documents carry a trusted timestamp.

A Docustay signature is a simple electronic signature with a strong record and a digital seal. There are no qualified signatures, no identity checks and no legal advice.

## Keep going with the next piece.

- [Tracking](/features/how-it-works#prove): The same events as a list and a CSV.
- [Signing](/features/how-it-works#sign): Settings that decide what ends up on the certificate.
- [Check a PDF](/verify): Drop a signed file on the verify page.

## Questions

**What if the time service is down?**

The file is still sealed, and the certificate says the timestamp was not added. We never claim a timestamp we do not have.

**Can I download the sealed copy again?**

Yes. It is stored with the audit trail, and everyone who signed was emailed a copy.

**Will every PDF viewer show the seal as valid?**

Some viewers show validity as unknown until they are told to trust our sealing certificate. The verify page is the supported way to check a file.

<!-- https://docustay.app/features/embedded-signing -->
# Signing inside your app.

Embedded e-signature shows the signing page, the builder and Scribe inside your own product. The signer never leaves your site, and you hear about it the moment they finish.

## The signer, the builder and Scribe.

**The signer.** Your page asks for a short-lived session for one seat and shows the signing page inside it.

**The builder.** Let your people build templates inside your own page, in the same editor Docustay uses. The session is made on your server and cannot send a document.

**Scribe.** Offer the document assistant as part of your own screens.

## From your server to a signed document.

1. **Your server**: Asks for a session
2. **Docustay**: Returns a short-lived address
3. **Your page**: Shows the signer
4. **Event**: completed reaches your code

## Only the websites you list.

Add the websites that may show the signer. Any other origin is refused, so nobody can frame your signing pages somewhere you did not agree to.

- An allow list under Developers, then Embedding.
- A framed page on an unlisted site shows a refusal, not the document.

## Six events, one handler.

```
<docustay-sign url="SESSION_URL"></docustay-sign>
<script>
  document.querySelector("docustay-sign").addEventListener("completed", (e) => console.log("signed", e.detail));
</script>
```

## What your page hears.

| Event | When it fires | What you do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ready | The form has loaded inside your page | Hide your loading state |
| waiting | It is not this person's turn yet | Show a message that someone else signs first |
| completed | The signer finished | Treat it as a prompt, then confirm on your server that the state is executed |
| declined | The signer declined | Record it and tell the sender |
| error | The link was refused: expired, wrong, or your website is not on the list | Ask your server for a fresh session |
| resize | The form's height changed | Resize the frame if you do not use auto-height |

## Plain HTML, React, Vue and Angular.

**A custom element.** Drop in the docustay-sign element and give it the session address. It works on any page with a script tag.

**Framework components.** React, Vue and Angular wrappers around the same element, each raising the same events.

**Your server.** The session is created on your server with a key, so no secret reaches the browser. The address is the only thing the page sees.

## What you do and what Docustay does.

- **Settings**: List the websites that may show the form, for example your app's address
- **Send**: Mark the seat as embedded so nobody is emailed for it
- **Server**: Ask for a session for one seat and one origin
- **Page**: Show the element and listen for completed

- **Session**: Returns an address that works for an hour for that seat
- **Frame**: Lets only the websites you listed show the form
- **Events**: Sends events to your page only on your listed website
- **Seal**: Seals the document and calls your webhook

## Let your people build templates in your own page.

The builder is the same editor Docustay uses, shown in a frame on your website. Your server asks for a builder session, your page shows it, and your code gets a template id when the person saves.

- The session key lives in the address fragment, so no server log sees it, and expires in an hour.
- It can read and write templates and nothing else. It cannot send a document.

## A refused frame cannot speak, so the element does.

Docustay sends a frame-ancestors header naming exactly the websites you listed, and only for a link made for an embedded seat. An ordinary emailed link can never be framed, even if someone adds embed=1 to it.

If nothing arrives from the frame after fifteen seconds, the element raises an error itself, because a refused frame cannot report that it was refused. Your page can then ask for a new session or show a plain message.

## Questions

**Which frameworks are supported?**

Plain HTML, plus React, Vue and Angular components.

**Can the signer need an account on my site?**

No. The signer needs only the session address your server asked for.

**What happens on a site I did not list?**

The page refuses to show the document.

**Does it work on a self-hosted install?**

Yes. Use your own address for the embed script, which is your install's web address followed by /embed/index.js.

**How long does a session last?**

An hour. Ask again each time the page loads. The five newest links for a seat keep working until their hour is up, so a page that reloads does not break a form that is already open.


## Keep reading

- [Test mode](/features/test-mode)
- [Your brand](/features/white-label)
- [Developers](/developers)

<!-- https://docustay.app/features/test-mode -->
# A full sandbox, built in.

E-signature test mode in one line: a test key signs watermarked documents and emails only you. Nothing a test key does counts toward a limit, and you can sign a test document yourself with one call.

## Practice runs that behave like the real thing.

**Test keys.** A key that starts dsk_test_ only does practice runs.

**Watermarked.** Every test document carries a TEST watermark so nobody mistakes it for a real agreement.

**Mail only to you.** Test emails go only to you, never to the signer you named.

## Same events, same webhooks.

**Same API.** A test key calls the same operations as a live key.

**Same events.** Test documents emit the same events, signed the same way, to your webhook.

**Not counted.** Test documents are left out of usage and billing.

## Listen to real events without opening a port.

**listen.** docustay listen forwards signed webhook events to your local server.

**send --test.** Sends a practice document and prints its id.

## Check the whole flow before anything real goes out.

**Your template.** See that fields land where you expect and that each seat is named the way your code names it.

**Your webhook receiver.** Prove that it verifies a delivery, ignores repeats and answers fast, with real signed events.

**Your embedded page.** Check that your page handles the form's events, and that your own screens show a finished document.

## A practice run should look like a practice run.

Because a test document is emailed only to you, you can send one to a made-up person and read the whole email yourself. It carries a TEST watermark and a [TEST] subject, so nobody mistakes it for a real agreement, and it is left out of usage and billing, so you can practise as much as you like.

When you are ready, switch to a live key, or turn the workspace's test setting off, and the same code sends real documents.

## Pick how you switch it on.

**A test key.** Use an API key that starts dsk_test_ and everything it sends is a practice run.

**A send option.** Send with test set to true from the app's own send step, for one document.

**A workspace setting.** Turn on Settings, Documents, Test mode and everything the workspace sends is a practice run until you turn it off.

## What differs between a test document and a live one.

|  | Test document | Live document |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Email goes to | Only the person who sent it, with [TEST] in the subject | The people you named |
| Pages carry | A TEST watermark | No watermark |
| Usage and billing | Left out | Counted |
| A signature | Records nothing as a real signature event | A real signature event |
| Events and webhooks | The same events, signed the same way | The same events |
| Plan needed | Any, including Free | Any |

## Send a test document in your language.

Every sample below was run against the API's own rules before it was published.

```
import { Docustay } from "@docustay2026/sdk";

const docustay = new Docustay(process.env.DOCUSTAY_API_KEY, process.env.DOCUSTAY_URL ? { baseUrl: process.env.DOCUSTAY_URL } : {});
const doc = await docustay.sendDocument({
  templateId: process.env.DOCUSTAY_TEMPLATE_ID,
  parties: [{ seat: "signer_1", name: "Rosa Alvarez", email: "rosa@example.com" }],
});
console.log(doc.id, doc.state);
```

## Prove your receiver without a real signature.

Test documents fire the same webhooks as live ones. From your laptop, listen forwards real, signed events to your own server, and trigger asks for a sample of any topic.

- Listen prints the secret to use and forwards each event.
- Verify checks one signature by hand when you give it the three headers and the exact body.

## What test mode does, and what it does not.

- **Whole flow**: Check your template, your webhook receiver and your embedded events
- **As often as you like**: Practice runs never count toward a limit
- **Same shape**: A send answers in the same shape as a live send

- **Payments**: It does not test payments against real cards
- **Real signers**: It never emails the person you named
- **Live proof**: A test signature is not a real signature event

## Questions

**Is test mode on Free?**

Yes. It is on every plan.

**Can a test document be sent to a real person?**

No. A test key emails only you.

**How do I test webhooks?**

Use the command line's listen command, or point a test key's webhook at a request catcher.

**Does a test signature count as a real one?**

No. Signing a test document records nothing as a real signature event, and the document is marked as a practice run on its pages and in the API.

**Can I test payments?**

Not against real cards. Test mode does not take payments.

**Where do I see a document's test flag?**

In the API the document carries test: true, and the app marks it with a Test chip and a banner on the signing page.

<!-- https://docustay.app/features/agent-ready -->
# AI agents draft. People send.

The MCP server e-signature tools and a Claude plugin let an assistant find documents, prepare drafts and read results. Sending takes a person, and a draft-only key makes that a rule.

## Look, prepare and report.

**Look.** Search documents, list payments and read the state of any document and its audit log.

**Prepare.** Make a draft from your words, a template and the people involved, check it, and revise it.

**Report.** Read results, download a finished copy to a folder on your own computer and summarise what is waiting on whom.

## Sending needs a person.

The MCP server shows a preview first and acts only on a second, confirmed call. A draft-only key can make drafts but cannot send them at all.

- No tool returns a signing link, a code or the key, and there is no tool to refund a payment.
- A read-only switch removes every tool that changes anything.

## Every action is on the record.

What an agent does is recorded like what a person does: which key, which document, and when. Revoke a key and its access ends at once.

- Per-key scopes decide what a key may do.
- The API call log keeps 30 days.

## What an assistant can and cannot do.

- **Find**: Search documents and read their state and audit log
- **Draft**: Make a draft from words, a template and the people, then check and revise it
- **Ask**: Propose a send, a reminder or a void, and show you the preview

- **Send alone**: Nothing is sent without a second, confirmed call
- **Reach the key**: No tool returns a signing link, a code or the key
- **Move money**: There is no tool to refund a payment

## Read, draft, and never send alone.

| Kind | Examples | Needs a person? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read | list_templates, get_document, get_audit_log, search_documents, list_payments | No |
| Prepare | create_document, use_template, check_document, revise_document, draft_document_with_ai | A person reviews the draft |
| Act | send_document, remind, void_document | Yes: a plain-words preview first, then a second call with confirm |
| Money | Refund a payment | Not offered as a tool at all |

## Add the server to your assistant.

```
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "docustay": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@docustay2026/mcp"],
      "env": { "DOCUSTAY_API_KEY": "dsk_test_..." }
    }
  }
}
```

## Rules that do not depend on the model behaving.

**Preview first.** send_document, remind and void_document do nothing the first time. They return a plain-words preview of who would be emailed, and only a second call with confirm acts.

**Draft-only keys.** A key made draft-only can create drafts and nothing else, whatever the assistant asks.

**Scoped keys.** Each key carries only the scopes you gave it, and you can revoke it at any time. A key without the scope gets the same plain refusal as any bad key.

## What it looks like to ask for a send.

You say: send the mutual NDA to Sam. The assistant finds the NDA, asks for a send without confirming, and shows you who would be emailed. You say yes, and only then does it send.

- Nothing is sent until the second call.
- No tool returns a signing link, a code or the key.

## A plugin that carries the know-how.

The Claude Code plugin bundles the server and five skills: sending for signature, text tags, embedded signing, webhooks and agent safety. The skills are plain Markdown files, so any agent that reads skill files can use them.

- For assistants that cannot run a program on your computer, a hosted connector does the same job.
- Everything the plugin does is recorded in the audit log.

## Questions

**Which assistants work?**

Any assistant that speaks the Model Context Protocol, and a Claude plugin that bundles the server.

**Can an agent send a document?**

Not on its own. A person approves each send.

**How many tools are there?**

39 tools in the MCP server, checked 12 October 2026. They cover reading, drafting, checking and acting, and every acting tool asks for a confirmation first.

**Can an assistant see signing links?**

No. No tool returns a signing link, a code or the key.

**Where do I get a key for an assistant?**

In the app, under Developers, API keys. Give it only the scopes it needs, and start with a test key.

**What about assistants that cannot run a program?**

A hosted connector does the same job for them.

**Is an assistant's work on the record?**

Yes. What an assistant does through a key is recorded like what a person does: which key, which document and when, in the same audit log your team reads. Revoke the key and its access ends at once.


## Keep reading

- [Scribe](/features/scribe)
- [Keys and scopes](/developers/keys-and-security)
- [Plays and Playbooks API](/developers/plays)

<!-- https://docustay.app/features/white-label -->
# Your logo, your colour.

Show your logo and your colour on the signing page and the documents, add a welcome note, and send every email under your name with your reply-to address. It is on every plan.

## Four things that carry your name.

**Logo and colour.** Documents and the signing page carry your logo and your brand colour.

**Welcome note.** A short note at the top of the signing page, in your words.

**Your name on every email.** Every email goes out under your sender name, with your reply-to address, so replies come to you.

**Letterhead and address.** Your address line and footer text appear where a document needs them.

## It reads as coming from you.

The email, the signing page and the certificate show your name, your logo and your colour. A small line says the document was sent with Docustay.

**From.** Your sender name, with your reply-to address.

**Look.** Your logo and colour.

## Need no Docustay mark at all?

To embed Docustay in your own product, resell it or keep a private fork, you need a commercial licence, from about $3,000 a year. A self-hosted install can also remove the footer and send from its own domain, mailbox or mail server.

- The hosted service always shows the Docustay line on signed copies.
- Self-host: remove the footer yourself, and use your own mail server.

## Three steps to your own look.

**Add your logo.** Upload your logo under Settings, Branding, and pick your brand colour.

**Write a welcome note.** A line or two at the top of the signing page, such as who is asking and why.

**Send a test.** Send a document to yourself with a test key and check the email, the signing page and the certificate.

## What changes, and what stays Docustay's.

- **Email**: Your sender name and reply-to address on every email
- **Signing page**: Your logo, your colour and your welcome note
- **One document**: The subject and message of a single send, and the reply-to and sender name from the API

- **Hosted**: A small Docustay line on signed copies, on every plan
- **Seal**: The sealing certificate belongs to Docustay
- **Records**: The audit trail format does not change

## Embed it, or run it yourself.

**Embedded signing.** Show the signer inside your own product so there is no Docustay page at all.

**Self-host.** Run the whole product on your own server under the AGPL-3.0, with your own domain, mail server and footer. A commercial licence covers resale and a private fork.

## Questions

**Is branding on Free?**

Yes. Your logo, colour, welcome note, sender name and reply-to address are on every plan.

**Can I remove the Docustay footer?**

Not on the hosted service. A self-hosted install can, and a commercial licence covers a fully white-labelled product.

**Can I embed instead?**

Yes. Embedded signing shows the signer inside your own product.

**Does branding cost extra?**

No. Your logo, colour, welcome note, sender name and reply-to address are on every plan.

**Can one document have its own subject and message?**

Yes. On the Details step of a send you can change the subject and the message for that document alone, and from the API you can set the reply-to address and the sender name.

<!-- https://docustay.app/self-host/requirements -->
# What you need to run it.

Six containers, one machine and Docker. A running install idles at about one gibibyte of memory with almost no CPU. Building the web image from source needs more than 3.8 GB.

## The numbers we have, and where they come from.

One real install, running for 44 hours with two documents in it, on a virtual machine with 3.8 GiB.

- **≈1.0 GiB** Memory, idle: All six containers together.
- **0 to 0.5%** CPU, idle: Measured across the same six containers.
- **>3.8 GB** Memory to build: The web image build was killed for lack of memory at 3.8 GB.
- **6** Containers: Database, file store, converter, app, worker and web.

## Where the memory goes.

| Container | What it does | Idle memory |
| --- | --- | --- |
| app | The API and the business logic | about 271 MiB |
| worker | Sends email and reminders | about 254 MiB |
| storage | The file store for signed PDFs, S3-compatible | about 176 MiB |
| gotenberg | Draws template pages to PDF | about 188 MiB |
| db | PostgreSQL 16 with row-level security | about 76 MiB |
| web | The app, the signing page and this kind of page | about 45 MiB |

## Two different jobs.

- **Memory**: About one gibibyte at idle
- **CPU**: Close to nothing at idle
- **Ports**: Only the web container publishes a port; the rest talk on Compose's private network
- **Address**: Put HTTPS in front and set the public address

- **Memory**: More than 3.8 GB: the web build was killed at 3.8 GB
- **Time**: The build that failed ran for about three minutes first
- **Advice**: Build on a bigger machine, or use a prebuilt image when one is published
- **Not measured**: The exact minimum to build

## We say so rather than guess.

**Load.** Memory and CPU with ten signers at once, or with the worker busy, have not been measured. The idle numbers are the lower bound.

**Disk.** Disk use depends on how many documents you keep. A signed PDF is small, and the database and file store sit in two named Docker volumes.

**Other platforms.** A Helm chart ships with requests of 256 Mi for the app and worker and 128 Mi for web. It has not been run on a cluster yet.

## A handful of lines in one file.

| Setting | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| KEYSTONE_PUBLIC_URL | The address people use. It goes into the links in emails, and the provider sends people back to it for single sign-on. |
| KEYSTONE_MASTER_KEY | Seals stored secrets and each workspace's file key. init.sh writes it. Lose it and sealed files cannot be opened. |
| RESEND_API_KEY | Your own mail provider key. Leave it empty to use your own SMTP server in Settings, Email. |
| KEYSTONE_MAIL_SENDER | The default From address until you verify your own domain. |
| KEYSTONE_TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS | How many proxies sit in front, so the real address of a visitor is read correctly. |
| DOCUSTAY_TELEMETRY | Set to off to stop the one anonymous daily ping. |

## Four things to have ready.

**Docker with Compose.** Any machine that runs Docker and Docker Compose. The install is a folder of files in the repository.

**A name and HTTPS.** A domain you control and a reverse proxy with a certificate in front of the web container. Caddy, nginx and Traefik are covered in the docs.

**Mail.** A provider key, or your own SMTP server including Amazon SES, so signers get their emails. Without one Docustay says email is not set up.

**A place for backups.** Somewhere that is not this machine. The backup folder holds secrets, so keep it as private as the install itself.

## One anonymous ping a day, and you can turn it off.

Once a day an install sends a random install id, its version and five counts, never content. Set DOCUSTAY_TELEMETRY=off to stop it, or send the report by hand. A Pro licence is checked the same way and keeps working up to 30 days offline.

- Nothing of ours is inside the install: every key and certificate is made on your machine.
- It is an honour system, not copy protection.

## Questions

**Can I run it on a small server?**

A running install idles at about one gibibyte, so a machine with 2 GB can run it. Building the web image needs more than 3.8 GB, so build elsewhere or use a prebuilt image.

**Does it need the internet?**

It needs outbound access for email and for the licence check if you run Pro, and a Pro licence keeps working up to 30 days offline. The Community edition needs no licence check.

**Which database does it use?**

PostgreSQL 16, in its own container, with row-level security on every table that holds workspace data.

**Where do I read the full steps?**

In the documentation: the install, the reverse proxy guide, backups, upgrades, single sign-on and hardening each have a page.

**Does a self-hosted install send my documents anywhere?**

No. Documents, files and keys stay on your machine, and the only thing the install sends us is the optional anonymous daily ping of a random id, the version and five counts.

- [Backups and upgrades](/self-host/backups-and-upgrades)
- [SSO and hardening](/self-host/sso-and-hardening)
- [Licensing](/licensing)

<!-- https://docustay.app/self-host/backups-and-upgrades -->
# Back up first. Then upgrade.

One script writes a dated folder with the database, the file store, the app data and your settings. Upgrading is three commands, and a backup comes before every one.

## Four files, all needed.

| File | What is in it | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| db.dump | The database as one consistent file | Every workspace, document record and setting |
| filedata.tgz | The file store volume | The signed PDFs and uploads, which are sealed |
| appdata.tgz | The app data volume | Keys and certificates made on your machine |
| env | Your settings file | The master key that opens the sealed files |

## One script, one dated folder.

Run it from the docustay folder. It checks that every file exists and is not empty, and says so if one is missing.

```
d="backup-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M)"; mkdir -p "$d"
docker compose exec -T db pg_dump -U docustay -Fc docustay > "$d/db.dump"
# then the two volumes as archives and a copy of .env, as in the backup guide
ls -l "$d"
```

## Why the four files go together.

**Files are sealed.** Every stored document file is encrypted under a key for its workspace, and that key is sealed by the master key in your settings file. A copy of the file store without the database cannot be opened.

**Same moment.** Take the database dump and the file archive at the same time, which the script does, so every file has the key that opens it.

**Check after a restore.** A short command reads up to 20 stored files for one workspace and prints whether each opens. It changes nothing.

## Seven steps on a new machine.

Do it once on a spare machine before you need it.

**Install and get the folder.** Install Docker and get the Docustay folder.

**Put the settings back.** Copy the saved env file back as .env so the master key is the same.

**Start once, then stop writers.** Let the install make its roles and tables, then stop everything that writes, and the file store as well.

**Load the database.** Empty what the first start created and load the dump.

**Load the volumes.** Unpack the two archives into their volumes.

**Start and check.** Start everything, check that every service is up and the app says healthy, and open a signed document.

## Carry out the deletions again.

A restore rewinds the database, so a person or a workspace deleted after the backup comes back with it. Every deletion Docustay carries out leaves one small entry in a ledger in the file store: a hash of the email address or the workspace id, the date and a request id, never a name.

- Run the replay script once to list what would be deleted again, then run it with apply to do it.
- It is safe to run twice: whatever is already gone is skipped.

## Three commands, then check.

Take a backup first. It is the only way back.

```
git pull
docker compose build
docker compose up -d
```

## What changes and what stays.

- **Database**: Keeps running; migrations apply on start
- **File store**: Restarts if its image changed; about twenty seconds not ready
- **Signing sessions**: A session in progress survives, and the page reloads once
- **Old images**: Remove them afterwards, they take several gigabytes

- **Back up**: Database, file store, app data and settings
- **Read**: The changelog for the versions in between
- **Keep**: Your secrets and your master key
- **Test**: Restore on a spare machine now and then

## Questions

**How often should I back up?**

Daily is a good start for the database. The file store changes only when documents are made or signed, so the same schedule is enough. Keep at least the last seven.

**What if I lose the settings file?**

The master key in it opens the sealed files, and a restore with a different key cannot open them. Keep the settings file in your backup and apart from the database dump if you encrypt it.

**Is there a way back from a bad upgrade?**

Yes: the backup you took first. Restore it, and the install is as it was.

**Can I test a restore without risking my live install?**

Yes, and you should. Do the restore on a spare machine, open a signed document and check that its files open, then do it again after a major upgrade. A backup you have not restored is a guess.

**Do I need to stop signing while I upgrade?**

No. A signing session in progress survives an upgrade, but the page reloads once, so it is kind to pick a quiet moment.

**What do I do after I restore?**

Check that the files open with the verify command, then replay the deletion ledger so that anyone deleted after the backup stays deleted. Open a signed document as a last check.


## Keep reading

- [Requirements](/self-host/requirements)
- [SSO and hardening](/self-host/sso-and-hardening)
- [Self-host](/self-host)

<!-- https://docustay.app/self-host/sso-and-hardening -->
# Sign in your way. Lock it down.

Connect your own OpenID Connect provider for single sign-on, then follow a short hardening list: private inside, HTTPS in front, encrypted disks and logs you control.

## What it does, and what it does not.

**Another way in.** It signs in people who already have an account on this install. It never creates one, so someone your provider vouches for but who has no account here is refused.

**Matched by email.** It matches by email address, and only when the provider says the address is verified.

**Nobody locked out.** Two-step rules are unchanged, and passwords keep working. Turning single sign-on on does not lock anyone out.

## Four settings and a restart.

At your provider make a client for Docustay with the sign-in redirect address set to your address plus /api/auth/oidc/callback.

```
DOCUSTAY_OIDC_ISSUER=https://sso.example.com/realms/main
DOCUSTAY_OIDC_CLIENT_ID=docustay
DOCUSTAY_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=<the client secret>
DOCUSTAY_OIDC_LABEL=Example SSO
```

## Three things people hit first.

| What you see | Why | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No email in the token | The provider keeps the email in its userinfo answer | Include the email scope |
| Provider does not vouch for the email | email_verified is not true | Turn on email verification at the provider |
| A button does not appear | The settings were not picked up | Recreate app, worker and web, then read the app log for lines that start oidc |

## Five variables, three of them required.

| Variable | Needed | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DOCUSTAY_OIDC_ISSUER | Yes | The address of your provider, for example a realm on your own identity server |
| DOCUSTAY_OIDC_CLIENT_ID | Yes | The client id you made for Docustay |
| DOCUSTAY_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET | Yes | The client secret; keep it as private as the other secrets in the settings file |
| DOCUSTAY_OIDC_LABEL | No | The name on the button, by default your identity provider |
| DOCUSTAY_OIDC_SCOPES | No | By default openid email profile; it must include openid and email |

## A standard flow, checked end to end.

The sign-in uses the authorization-code flow with PKCE, a state value and a nonce. The identity token is verified for its signature, issuer, audience, nonce and expiry, and a short-lived cookie holds the state between your click and the provider's reply.

Single sign-on turns on only when the issuer, client id and client secret are all set. It is for self-hosted installs with the built-in identity, and invited people only: an unknown email is refused.

## Seven parts of a hardening list.

**Security settings.** Set the workspace's own security settings, including whether an owner requires two-step sign-in for the whole team.

**Keep the inside private.** Only the web container listens. The database, file store and converter talk on Compose's private network.

**Encrypt what is stored.** Put the volumes on an encrypted disk, keep the master key safe, and encrypt each backup before it leaves the machine.

**Choose your providers.** Your own mail, your own sign-in and, if documents must not leave your servers, no AI key at all.

**Sign-in and sessions.** Offer two-step to everyone, and list or end any session under Settings, Security.

**Logs and monitoring.** Logs leave out email addresses and credentials; send them to a store you control and set an alert address.

## HTTPS in front, one port out.

- **Proxy**: Put HTTPS in front with Caddy, nginx or Traefik
- **Address**: Set the public address to the https address
- **Firewall**: Allow 443, and 80 for the certificate check; nothing else from outside

- **Ports**: Do not publish the database or the file store
- **Telemetry**: Switch the one anonymous ping off if you must
- **Updates**: Do not skip upgrades: release notes say when a fix is about security

## Questions

**Does single sign-on create accounts?**

No. It only signs in people who already have an account on the install, so invite them first.

**Can I use passkeys?**

Yes, once you turn them on with the passkey settings in your environment file.

**Does the install call out to AI?**

Only if you set an AI key. Leave it empty if documents must not leave your servers for drafting.

**Where do I read the whole list?**

In the hardening guide and the single sign-on guide in the documentation.

**Do people need a password if they use single sign-on?**

No, because it replaces the password step, but passwords keep working for anyone who has one, so turning single sign-on on locks nobody out. Two-step rules are unchanged.

**Which providers work?**

Any provider that speaks OpenID Connect with the authorization-code flow and PKCE, such as a Keycloak realm. Register the redirect address that ends in the callback path and give the client id and secret to the install.

**Is single sign-on on the hosted service?**

No. Single sign-on is for self-hosted installs with the built-in identity, where you run your own provider and your own settings.

**What do the logs contain?**

Server and worker logs leave out email addresses and credentials. Keep that on, send the logs to a store you control and keep them as long as your policy says.


## Keep reading

- [Requirements](/self-host/requirements)
- [Backups and upgrades](/self-host/backups-and-upgrades)
- [Trust](/trust)

# Whatever needs a signature.

Pick the kind of paperwork you send. Each page shows the templates that fit and how it goes.

## Seven places people start.

- [Contracts that get signed](/use-cases/contracts): Send an agreement and let everyone sign from a link.
- [NDAs signed in minutes](/use-cases/ndas): Send a non-disclosure agreement before the first conversation.
- [Waivers and consent](/use-cases/waivers-and-consent): Send a waiver to each person before an event or an activity.
- [HR paperwork and onboarding](/use-cases/hr-and-onboarding): Send the offer, then the first-day paperwork, to each new person as a package they can sign in one sitting.
- [Leases and rental applications](/use-cases/real-estate): Collect the application, then send the addendum and the deposit agreement.
- [Permission slips and school forms](/use-cases/education): Send a permission slip to every family at once.
- [Statements of work and client agreements](/use-cases/agencies): Send the scope, then each change to it, then the deposit.

## Every use case is the same short path.

Pick a template or describe one. Send it to the people who sign. Each signs in turn or all at once, and everyone keeps the sealed copy.

**Start.** Pick from 54 built-in templates, or describe your own and review what Scribe builds.

**Sign.** No account for the signer, any device.

**Keep.** A sealed PDF and a certificate, with every step in the audit log.

## What every one of these includes.

- **54** built-in templates: Roles and fields placed.
- **0** accounts for the signer: They open a link.
- **15** documents a month, free: 

## Pick the one closest to your job.

Each page names the templates for that work, what to check before you send, and what you keep afterwards.

**Contracts.** Services agreements, contractor agreements and the paperwork around a job. Two parties sign, in order or together, and both keep a sealed copy.

**NDAs.** A mutual NDA and a non-solicitation agreement for the start of a deal. Both sides sign from a link on any device, with no account.

**Waivers and consent.** Liability waivers, photo and media releases and permission slips, sent to each person on a list, with a record for everyone who signs.

**HR and onboarding.** Offer letters and a first-day pack the new person fills in on a phone before they arrive, with one signed copy for the file.

**Real estate.** Lease addenda, rental applications and deposit agreements, sent to each applicant or tenant on their own, with the deposit paid inside the document.

**Education.** Permission slips and consent paperwork sent to every family from a list, so you can see at a glance who has answered and who has not.

**Agencies.** Statements of work and change orders, so each job and each change has its own signed scope and price.

## The same sealed record, whichever one you use.

Every use case ends the same way, so you only learn it once.

**A sealed PDF.** When everyone has signed, the finished PDF is sealed with a digital signature over the whole file, so a later change shows.

**A certificate on the last page.** It lists who signed and when, and carries a hash of the file, so the copy can be checked on the verify page without an account.

**An audit trail you can export.** Every step on a document is recorded, from sent to opened to signed, and the trail exports as a CSV.

## Questions

**Is there a template for everything?**

No. There are 54 built-in templates. Describe a different document and Scribe writes it; you review it before it goes out.

**Is a template legal advice?**

No. It is a starting point in plain words.

<!-- https://docustay.app/use-cases/contracts -->
# Contracts that get signed

Send an agreement and let everyone sign from a link. You keep one sealed copy and the record of who signed when.

## Flip through the pages first.

Each card is the real document: its pages, its fields, its wording.

- [Service agreement template](/templates/service-agreement-template)
- [Independent contractor agreement template](/templates/independent-contractor-agreement-template)
- [Vendor agreement template](/templates/vendor-agreement-template)

## Three agreements people send most.

**Service agreement.** Scope, fees and term between a provider and a client.

**Independent contractor.** Who does the work, how it is paid, and who owns the result.

**Vendor agreement and SOW.** Terms for a supplier, then a statement of work for each job.

## How it goes.

For example, a studio sends a services agreement to a client on Monday, the client signs on a phone that afternoon, and both sides have the sealed PDF before the first invoice.

1. **Draft**: Template or Scribe
2. **Send**: Link by email
3. **Sign**: Any device
4. **Keep**: Sealed copy + record

## A copy you can stand behind.

**Sealed copy.** One PDF with every signature, sealed so a later change shows.

**Certificate.** Who signed, when and from where, on the last page.

**Audit log.** Each step in order, exportable as a CSV.

## Two parties, eight pages, every field placed.

The Provider and the Client each have their own fields. Initials go on every page, and the signatures and dates are at the end.


## One agreement, four steps.

**Place or keep the fields.** Start from the template with its fields in place, or change them.

**Send it.** The email names who asked and carries one button.

**They sign.** On a phone or a computer, with no account.

**You both keep it.** A sealed PDF with a certificate of who signed and when.

## Everyone who sends contracts, on one price.

Give each person a role. The team sees its own documents. Pro is one flat price for the whole workspace; Pay as you go charges for each team member you add.

**Price.** Pro is flat for the workspace; Pay as you go is $5 per team member a month.

## Six templates that cover most agreements.

Each one has its roles and fields placed already. Start from the one that fits and change anything that does not.

**Independent contractor agreement template.** Who does the work, how it is paid, who owns the result. Company and Contractor each sign their own boxes, over 4 pages and 31 fields, about 10 minutes in all.

**Service agreement template.** Scope, fees and term between a provider and a client. Provider and Client each sign their own boxes, over 8 pages and 58 fields, about 20 minutes in all.

**Vendor agreement template.** Terms for a supplier you will buy from again. Company and Vendor each sign their own boxes, over 6 pages and 50 fields, about 17 minutes in all.

**Mutual release agreement.** Both sides let go of claims against each other. Party A, Party B and Witness each sign their own boxes, over 3 pages and 18 fields, about 7 minutes in all.

**Referral agreement template.** A fee for sending you a client. Company and Referrer each sign their own boxes, over 3 pages and 16 fields, about 7 minutes in all.

**Equipment loan agreement.** What was lent, to whom, and when it comes back. Lender and Borrower each sign their own boxes, over 3 pages and 24 fields, about 9 minutes in all.

## What the document asks for.

Read from the template itself, so this list is what the signer will see.

**What the independent contractor agreement asks for.** Company name, Contractor’s name, Start date, Company’s legal name, Company address, Contractor’s full name, Contractor’s address, Describe the services, How the Contractor is paid, Amount, in US dollars, How often the Contractor invoices, Days to pay, Notice period, Include the non-solicitation section, and 17 more. Each box sits where it belongs on the page and belongs to one person, so nobody fills in a part that is not theirs.

**What the service agreement asks for.** Provider’s name, Client’s name, Date of this Agreement, Provider’s legal name, Client’s legal name, Provider’s address, Client’s address, Provider’s email, Client’s email, Time to review, Days to pay an invoice, Notice to end for convenience, Include the non-solicitation section, Governing law (state), and 44 more. Each box sits where it belongs on the page and belongs to one person, so nobody fills in a part that is not theirs.

**What the vendor agreement asks for.** Company name, Vendor name, Date of this Agreement, Company’s legal name, Company address, Vendor’s legal name, Vendor address, Inspection period, Notice of a price change, Payment terms, Amount of cover, in US dollars, a fixed amount, in US dollars, Initial term, Notice not to renew, and 36 more. Each box sits where it belongs on the page and belongs to one person, so nobody fills in a part that is not theirs.

**What the mutual release agreement asks for.** Date of this Release, First party’s name, Second party’s name, Describe what is being settled, Settlement terms, if any, Payment and when it is due, if any, What either side may say, Days to consider this Release, Governing law (state), Printed name, Party A signature, Party A date signed, Party B signature, Party B date signed, and 4 more. Each box sits where it belongs on the page and belongs to one person, so nobody fills in a part that is not theirs.

**What the referral agreement asks for.** Start date, Company, Referrer, Time to confirm a Referral, Time to become a customer, The reward, such as a percentage or a fixed amount, Reward paid within, Governing law (state), Printed name, Title or capacity, Company signature, Company date signed, Referrer signature, Referrer date signed, and 2 more. Each box sits where it belongs on the page and belongs to one person, so nobody fills in a part that is not theirs.

**What the equipment loan agreement asks for.** Date of this agreement, Lender’s name, Borrower’s name, Item and make, Serial number or tag, Accessories, such as cables and cases, Estimated replacement value, in US dollars, Condition, Notes on condition, I agree that the condition is as described, Lend date, Return by, Where to return it, the purpose, such as a project or event, and 10 more. Each box sits where it belongs on the page and belongs to one person, so nobody fills in a part that is not theirs.

## Check these before an agreement goes out.

Most delays come from a missing name, a wrong date or the wrong person receiving it.

**Who signs, and in what order.** Decide whether the signers go one at a time or all at once. One at a time suits an agreement the client reviews after you have signed; all at once is quicker when nothing depends on order.

**Fields only you can fill.** Some boxes, such as your own name and the date of the agreement, are filled in by you before sending, so the other side never has to. The template marks them as yours.

## While the agreement is out.

You can see where it stands without asking anyone.

**See who has opened it.** Each document shows whether it was sent, opened or signed, and by whom. If a signer has not opened it, you know before you chase them.

**Let reminders do the chasing.** Reminders go out on their own until everyone has signed, so a forgotten email does not hold up the start date.

**Signers need no account.** The signer opens the link on a phone or a computer, reads, draws or types a signature and finishes. There is nothing to install and no password.

## Once it is signed, it is findable.

The record does not end at the last signature.

**Everyone keeps a copy.** Both parties receive the sealed PDF with its certificate. You can download it again from the document at any time.

**Send the same agreement again.** Save your own copy of the template with your wording and fields, and the next client starts from that. Free makes up to 5 new templates a month; the paid plans have no limit.

## Questions

**Can I change the wording?**

Yes. Your copy of a template is yours to edit before you send it. Nothing in it is legal advice.

**Can both sides sign in order?**

Yes. Set the provider to sign first, or let both sign at once.

**Can Scribe draft one that is not listed?**

Describe a different one and Scribe writes it; you review it before it is sent.

<!-- https://docustay.app/use-cases/ndas -->
# NDAs signed in minutes

Send a non-disclosure agreement before the first conversation. Both sides sign from a link, and both keep the sealed copy.

## Flip through the pages first.

Each card is the real document: its pages, its fields, its wording.

- [NDA template](/templates/nda-template)
- [Non-solicitation agreement](/templates/non-solicitation-agreement)

## Three things for the start of a deal.

**NDA.** Both parties promise to keep what they share private.

**Non-solicitation agreement.** A promise not to hire away each other's people.

**In your own name.** Email carries your logo and your name.

## How it goes.

For example, a founder sends a mutual NDA before a first call, the other side signs from a link, and both keep a copy with its certificate.

1. **Pick**: NDA template
2. **Send**: To the other side
3. **Sign**: Both sign
4. **Keep**: Certificate

## A copy you can stand behind.

**Sealed copy.** One PDF with every signature, sealed so a later change shows.

**Certificate.** Who signed, when and from where, on the last page.

**Audit log.** Each step in order, exportable as a CSV.

## Short enough to read, complete enough to sign.

Two parties, three pages, with the parties' details on the first page and a signature and date for each at the end.


## In order, or both at once.

Set Party A to sign first, or let both sign together. When the second signature lands, the sealed copy exists.

**Quick.** No account, any device.

**Provable.** The certificate lists each signature with its time.

## The other side signs from a phone.

They open the link, read it, tick that they agree to sign electronically and finish.

**Reminders.** Reminders go out until they have signed, and stop when they do.

## An NDA and a promise not to recruit.

The two documents most deals start with, both already set up for two signers.

**NDA template.** Both sides keep what they share private. Party A and Party B each sign their own boxes, over 3 pages and 25 fields, about 8 minutes in all.

**Non-solicitation agreement.** A promise not to hire away each other's people. Company and Employee each sign their own boxes, over 3 pages and 14 fields, about 6 minutes in all.

## What the document asks for.

Read from the template itself, so this list is what the signer will see.

**What the nda asks for.** First party’s name, Second party’s name, Effective date, Party A’s legal name, Party A’s address, Party B’s legal name, Party B’s address, the purpose, in a sentence or two, Sharing period, Protection period, Governing law (state), Printed name, Title or capacity, Party A signature, and 11 more. Each box sits where it belongs on the page and belongs to one person, so nobody fills in a part that is not theirs.

**What the non-solicitation agreement asks for.** Company name, Employee’s full name, Company’s legal name, Date, Employee’s role, Period after leaving, Governing law (state), Printed name, Employee signature, Employee date signed, Title or capacity, Company signature, Company date signed, and 1 more. Each box sits where it belongs on the page and belongs to one person, so nobody fills in a part that is not theirs.

## The three decisions an NDA turns on.

An NDA is short, so the details that matter are few. Settle them before you send.

**One-way or mutual.** A mutual NDA binds both sides to the same promise, which is easier to ask for and quicker to agree. If only one side will share secrets, change the wording so it says so before you send it.

**Where the other side signs.** Many NDAs are signed by someone who is travelling or between meetings. The signing page works on a phone with no account, so you are not waiting for a laptop.

## While you wait for the other side.

An NDA is usually urgent: the conversation cannot start until it is signed.

**Send in your own name.** The email carries your logo and goes out under your name, so the other side sees a message from you and not from a stranger.

**Choose the order.** You can have the other side sign first, or both sign at once. Everyone at once is the fastest way to get the document back.

**Know when it is opened.** The document shows when it was opened and by whom, so a quiet signer is a reminder you can send, not a mystery.

## What you keep after both sides sign.

If a dispute ever comes up, the record is what you will want.

**A sealed copy with a certificate.** The signed PDF is sealed so a later change shows, and its last page records who signed and when, with a hash of the file.

**Proof anyone can check.** The verify page checks a signed PDF in the browser, with no account. You can give it to the other side or an adviser.

**A note on what it is.** A Docustay signature is a simple electronic signature with a strong record and a digital seal. The template is a starting point in plain words and is not legal advice.

## Questions

**Who signs first?**

You choose. One at a time, or both together.

**Can the other side sign on a phone?**

Yes. They open the link and sign, with no account.

**Is the NDA legal advice?**

No. It is a starting point in plain words. Change what does not fit before you send it.
